To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) binary networks have a qualitatively different phase transition between ordered/chaotic network behavior than analog networks; (ii) the memory function of binary networks decreases with increasing network density; (iii) the computational performance of analog and binary networks are comparable for small network densities.

(1) binary networks with low connectivity perform better than analog networks, and (2) the memory function of binary networks is bounded by the mean field predictor, which in turn is a function of the connectivity.

the differences in performance between analog and binary neurons are rooted in the differences in the dynamics and connectivity structure of the networks, and that the performance of binary networks can be predicted with the help of mean field techniques.
the computational performance of binary RC systems can be increased by reducing the connectivity, but that this comes with a loss in the memory of the network.

the computational performance of RC systems with analog neurons is robust against variations in the network connectivity, while RC systems with binary neurons show a strong dependence on the connectivity.

the differences between the two RC implementations are not as fundamental as previously thought, and that they can be understood in terms of differences between the integration timescales in analog and binary circuits.
